transcript: [00:00] Samira Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samira from Redwood Inference. We'll do a quick hosted API demo for chat and text generation basics, and Jordan will jump into streaming and retry details.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Hi, Maya here. We're interested in how we can get low latency for patient-facing chat and what the retry story looks like. We also need a sense of cost.

[00:25] Samira Patel: Great, high level first — our Hosted API gives you generation, chat, embeddings. For chat we surface a simple endpoint that supports streaming, function calling, and structured outputs. We'll demo a couple of SDK snippets after the console tour.

[00:42] Jordan Lee: Quick tech note — streaming is chunked by token groups; you can start rendering as tokens arrive. We support client-side reconnects and server-side retries; we recommend idempotency keys for safe retries on create-like requests.
[01:05] Tom Reynolds: When you say chunked, is it deltas or full message patches?

[01:10] Jordan Lee: Mostly deltas. So you get incremental text, and metadata events for function calls or end-of-stream. Some transcriptions may say key cache as kv-cache but it's the same concept, sorry for the jargon slip earlier.
[02:00] (crosstalk) Ravi Kumar: What's the overhead for streaming vs non-streaming?

[02:05] Jordan Lee: Streaming adds small per-chunk overhead but improves perceived latency since you can start rendering at say 50-100ms depending on model & prompt. For p99 it's model + network bound; we provide per-route timing in the console so you can see token-level breakdowns.

[03:12] Samira Patel: I'll share a quick demo request. Example curl: POST /v1/chat/completions with body: model: "redwood-medium", messages: [...], stream: true. You can also set temperature, top_p, max_tokens. Jordan will show an SDK snippet after this.

[04:00] Jordan Lee: Important params: temperature (0-1), top_p for nucleus sampling, and max_tokens controls length. For deterministic outputs use temperature 0 and set top_p low plus a fixed seed on supported models. Note some open checkpoints don't support seeds — we'll point that out.
[05:20] Elena Santos: From security — where does the data go? Is it retained? What's the retention policy?

[05:30] Samira Patel: Hosted API has default 30-day log retention for traces; you can opt out of retention for request payloads in enterprise plans. We also offer KMS integration for key management and SOC2 compliance — happy to send the security pack.
[06:10] Maya Chen: Do you support SSO and RBAC for team access?
[06:15] Samira Patel: Yes, SAML SSO and role-based access controls in the Console. We also have audit logs per request that can be exported.

[07:02] Jordan Lee: Back to retries — best practice: use an idempotency key header like X-Idempotency-Key. For streaming reconnects, the SDK will attempt to resume where possible; otherwise the server returns a retryable error code (5xx) and client can retry safely with the key.
[08:30] Ravi Kumar: How do you handle partial outputs on retries? If a user sees half the message then we retry, will we duplicate content?

[08:40] Jordan Lee: Good question — idempotency keys de-duplicate server-side; if you re-POST with same key and the call completed previously, the server returns the original response. For long-running streaming sessions we recommend checkpointing at function-call boundaries.
[09:55] Tom Reynolds: Can you demo a real SDK streaming example?

[10:02] Jordan Lee: Sure — here's Node pseudo-code. client.chat.stream({model: 'redwood-medium', messages, temperature: 0.2, idempotency_key: uuid()}). on('token', t => render(t)). on('done', ()=>...). I'll paste this in the chat. Note: our SDK also exposes backoff/retry policy hooks.
[11:40] (Jordan pastes link to quickstart repo) link: https://github.com/redwood/quickstart-streaming
[12:15] Maya Chen: If we want deterministic behavior for certain flows (like templated responses), is it better to use non-streaming with temperature 0?
[12:22] Jordan Lee: Yes, non-streaming with temperature 0 yields more deterministic results. Streaming is orthogonal; you can stream deterministic outputs too as long as model settings are fixed.

[13:50] Samira Patel: Cost considerations — we bill per output token for hosted. Batching and caching (prefix cache) can drastically reduce token costs for repeated prompts. Our Optimize tooling suggests batching/quantization configs.
[14:30] Ravi Kumar: We have a lot of repetitive prompts for triage — can caching help?
[14:35] Jordan Lee: Absolutely — prefix caching caches KV states for repeated prefixes. That reduces compute and latency. The Console can show hit/miss rates and recommend cache TTLs.
[15:40] Elena Santos: About compliance — do you provide data residency controls? We can't send PHI out of region easily.

[15:48] Samira Patel: We have region-scoped endpoints and Private deployment for strict residency. For hosted, we can limit processing to specific cloud regions; for fully on-prem or VPC, we offer Redwood Private.
[16:55] Maya Chen: How do you handle model rollouts and fallback? If a model is overloaded or updated, what's the behavior?

[17:05] Jordan Lee: Smart routing policy: we route by latency, cost, and region. Automatic fallback to compatible model variants if primary model hits capacity. You can pin a model version for consistency or allow automatic fallback for availability.
[18:30] Tom Reynolds: Any pitfalls with stop sequences we should watch for?

[18:36] Jordan Lee: Stop sequences are respected but can be approximate if tokenizer boundaries don't align. Test with your prompt sets; our eval tooling can run prompt sets to flag stop-sequence failures.

[19:50] (Samira shares console screen) We're in the Console > Routes. You can see per-route latency, cost, token breakdown, sample traces. Here is a streaming session trace — notice partial token events and the breakdown by kernel time vs queue time.
[21:10] Maya Chen: That trace view is helpful. Can we export these traces to our observability?
[21:18] Samira Patel: Yes, webhook or direct export to DataDog/BigQuery/export buckets. We also include token-level timestamps if you need precise p99 analysis.
[22:25] Ravi Kumar: For benchmarking, what should we provide?

[22:30] Jordan Lee: Two things: representative prompt set and target concurrency/throughput. We'll run a dedicated benchmark on Hosted with your prompts and return p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens. If you need absolute isolation, we can propose Dedicated pools.
[23:10] Tom Reynolds: Is there a free sandbox we can try?
[23:14] Samira Patel: Yes, the self-serve account includes credits and quickstart templates. I'll include a guided repo and sample prompts.
[24:05] (short silence, typing)
[24:40] Jordan Lee: A small note about backpressure: if you're rendering tokens live, implement a token queue on the client and handle reconnect/backoff. Our SDK does basic buffering for you.
[25:55] Elena Santos: Do you offer contractual guarantees around data handling?
[26:02] Samira Patel: Yes, enterprise agreements include data handling terms, no-retention options, KMS controls, and SOC2 attestations. We'll attach the security packet to the next email.
[27:30] Maya Chen: Any limits on token size or message history? We have long context use-cases.
[27:38] Jordan Lee: Models have max context windows — older models 4k/8k, newer up to 64k depending on variant. We also support streaming KV cache to handle long histories more efficiently.
[28:50] Ravi Kumar: How do retries interact with billing? If we retry, are we double-billed?

[28:58] Jordan Lee: We try to avoid double-billing on client retries if the server completed the request — idempotency keys return the original response. If you do a duplicate request that actually executes twice, then yes, two billable runs. We'll show instrumentation to detect that.

[30:10] Samira Patel: Quick demo of edge-case: setting temperature high for more creative summaries, watch tokens cost increase and latency slightly. We recommend different profiles by route: generation vs classification.
[31:35] Tom Reynolds: Can Optimize suggest quantization or model variant changes?

[31:40] Jordan Lee: Yes, Optimize gives recommendations: for throughput-sensitive workloads it might recommend an 8-bit quantized variant or a smaller family model, and shows estimated cost/latency delta.
[33:12] Maya Chen: If we wanted to trial Dedicated capacity later, how does the transition look?

[33:20] Samira Patel: Smooth — same API surface. You can pin models and move a route to Dedicated. Billing shifts to reserved capacity model with commit tiers. We'll propose numbers after the benchmark.
[34:50] (Jordan pastes link to security pack) link: https://redwood.ai/security-pack.pdf
[35:20] Elena Santos: Thanks, we'll review. Any regulatory certifications?
[35:26] Samira Patel: SOC2 in place; ISO in progress for certain regions. Specific compliance packages can be attached to enterprise contracts.
[36:45] Ravi Kumar: For the benchmark, can you run with streaming enabled so we can measure perceived latency?
[36:53] Jordan Lee: Absolutely — we'll run both streaming and non-streaming and report both p99 server completion and first-byte latency for streaming.
[38:10] Tom Reynolds: What's the best way to instrument retries from our side?
[38:15] Jordan Lee: Use SDK hooks to log idempotency keys and response status; we recommend exponential backoff with jitter. We'll include a sample interceptor in the SDK snippet.
[39:40] Maya Chen: One more — rate limits. We have bursty traffic during triage windows. How do you recommend handling that?
[39:48] Samira Patel: Use the Console to configure per-route quotas and burst allowances. For production we can provision dedicated capacity or burst credits on Hosted for known windows.

[41:00] (Samira summarizes) Recap: we'll send pricing + SLA, Jordan will share streaming SDK + retry examples, AtlasHealth will send prompt set and latency targets. We'll schedule a technical deep dive if Dedicated or Private are needed.
[41:28] Ravi Kumar: Sounds good. Can we get an example of the idempotency header in curl?
[41:35] Jordan Lee: curl -H 'X-Idempotency-Key: 123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000' -d '{...}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/completions
[42:10] Tom Reynolds: Any gotchas for stop tokens in multi-language prompts?
[42:18] Jordan Lee: Tokenizers differ by language; tests help. Use explicit stop sequences and validate with our eval tooling. We'll run your multi-language prompts in the benchmark.
[43:40] Maya Chen: Appreciate the fast demo. We'll look at the quickstart and expect the benchmark results.
[43:50] Samira Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and pricing. Expect email with attachments by end of day Monday.
[44:10] (meeting winding down, small talk)
[44:35] Elena Santos: Thanks — looking forward to the security docs.
[45:00] Samira Patel: Thank you all, bye.
